interview.q: Why does the dtype belong to the array rather than to each element?
interview.answer: One dtype per array lets NumPy store raw values in a typed buffer and pick a compiled loop for arithmetic. Per-element types would mean per-element checks, which is exactly the list overhead NumPy removes.

interview.q: How does slicing a large array avoid copying memory?
interview.answer: A slice only stores an offset, a shape and strides over the same buffer. No values move, so slicing a gigabyte costs a few numbers.

interview.q: Why does `np.array([1, 2.0])` contain floats?
interview.answer: A single array needs one dtype, and NumPy promotes the integers to the common type float64 rather than keeping mixed values.

defense.q: Defend using NumPy for a signal that must be filtered many times.
defense.answer: The filter runs as vectorised arithmetic over one buffer, and repeated passes avoid per-element Python overhead. The same array can be reused without re-wrapping values.

defense.q: Two arrays print the same numbers but behave differently. Explain why dtype is the reason.
defense.answer: One may be integer and the other float, so division, overflow and equality all differ. Printing hides the dtype that decides those results.

defense.q: Defend choosing an ndarray over a DataFrame for a single numeric column.
defense.answer: There is nothing to label or align, so the frame only adds index bookkeeping. An array is smaller and its operations are the primitive ones the frame calls anyway.

interview.q: How do you read a shape of `(2, 3, 4)` in words?
interview.answer: Two blocks, each holding three rows of four values. Reading right to left gives the fastest-varying axis first.

interview.q: What is `size` in terms of `shape`?
interview.answer: The product of the shape entries. An empty axis makes the product zero.

interview.q: Why is `len(arr)` not the number of elements?
interview.answer: `len` reports the length of the first axis only, so a `(2, 3)` array has `len` 2 and size 6.

defense.q: Defend asserting `ndim` at a function boundary.
defense.answer: A function written for 2-D input silently misbehaves on 3-D data by reducing the wrong axis. The assertion turns that into an immediate error.

defense.q: Explain why a 3-D array is not "three lists".
defense.answer: It is one buffer addressed by three strides, so it can be sliced, transposed and broadcast as a single object. Three lists would be three objects with no shared shape.

defense.q: Defend naming axes in comments instead of using bare axis numbers.
defense.answer: `axis=1` is meaningless without the shape in mind, and a wrong axis is a silent wrong answer. A comment such as `# axis 1 = features` is the cheapest guard.

interview.q: Why does `np.full` take a shape but `np.full_like` does not?
interview.answer: `full_like` copies the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is why it takes that array instead of a shape.

interview.q: What does `np.arange(5).reshape(1, -1)` produce?
interview.answer: A single row with five columns: the `1` fixes the row count and `-1` infers the columns.

interview.q: Why is `np.zeros` slower than `np.empty`?
interview.answer: `zeros` writes every element; `empty` only allocates, leaving whatever bytes were there.

defense.q: Defend `linspace` for a fixed number of dashboard points.
defense.answer: The chart needs exactly N points across a closed range, and `linspace` guarantees the count and both endpoints without floating-step drift.

defense.q: Why does `np.eye(3)` print floats?
defense.answer: The default dtype is float64, because an identity is usually used in floating-point algebra. Pass `dtype=int` for an integer one.

defense.q: Defend building an index array once and reusing it.
defense.answer: Positions rarely change while data does, so recomputing them wastes work and risks drift. One array documents the layout the rest of the code assumes.

interview.q: What do you gain and lose with `dtype="int8"`?
interview.answer: Four times less memory than int64, at the cost of a range of only -128 to 127, so overflow becomes possible.

interview.q: What happens to a float array cast to `int32`?
interview.answer: Each value is truncated toward zero, losing the fractional part without warning.

interview.q: Why is `0.1 + 0.2` not exactly `0.3` in float64?
interview.answer: Neither decimal is representable exactly in binary, so the stored approximations add to a value one bit away from the nearest 0.3.

defense.q: Defend float64 until a calculation reaches a money boundary.
defense.answer: Intermediate work needs precision, and rounding should happen once, deliberately, at the boundary. Rounded intermediate values compound error.

defense.q: Explain why `int + float` promoting to float64 surprises people.
defense.answer: The dtype changes silently, so later integer division or exact equality no longer behaves as before. The promotion is correct, but it is not obvious.

defense.q: Defend stating a dtype contract in a data loader.
defense.answer: Every downstream step inherits the dtype, so declaring it once prevents implicit promotions and documents the memory budget.

interview.q: What does a negative index select?
interview.answer: A position counted from the end, so `-1` is the last element and `-len` is the first.

interview.q: How do you select a diagonal with two index arrays?
interview.answer: Pass the same positions twice, `arr[np.arange(n), np.arange(n)]`, which pairs them elementwise.

interview.q: Why is `arr[mask]` a copy while `arr[1:3]` is not?
interview.answer: A boolean mask selects arbitrary positions, so the result cannot be described with strides. A basic slice can.

defense.q: Defend `arr[:, None]` when keeping a selected column 2-D.
defense.answer: It preserves the column axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts across columns. Dropping to 1-D silently changes what later arithmetic aligns with.

defense.q: Explain why a row-selection mask must be 1-D.
defense.answer: It selects positions along axis 0, one boolean per row. A 2-D mask would select cells, which is a different operation.

defense.q: Defend fancy indexing for drawing a shuffled batch.
defense.answer: An integer array of row positions gathers exactly those rows in the requested order, with no loop and no assumption about contiguity.

interview.q: What is the difference between `arr[::2]` and `arr[1::2]`?
interview.answer: The first takes even positions starting at 0; the second starts at 1 and takes every second value after it.

interview.q: How do you reverse only the rows of a 2-D array?
interview.answer: Use `arr[::-1]`, which flips axis 0 and leaves the columns in order.

interview.q: Why does `arr[2:2]` return an empty array instead of raising?
interview.answer: A slice with equal bounds is a legal empty selection, not an error, which keeps loop code simple.

defense.q: Defend clamping slice bounds in a parser.
defense.answer: Input lengths vary, and Python slicing already clamps, so explicit `min(n, len(a))` documents the intent without changing behaviour.

defense.q: Explain why writing to `arr[:, 0]` changes every reference to that array.
defense.answer: The column is a view on the shared buffer, so assignment writes real memory rather than a copy. Any other name for that array sees it.

defense.q: Defend a negative-step slice over `np.flip` when trimming.
defense.answer: It expresses the reversal without a function call and returns a view, so it is cheaper when no copy is needed.

interview.q: What does `reshape` require about the element count?
interview.answer: The target shape must hold exactly the same number of elements, or NumPy raises instead of padding.

interview.q: How do you add a batch axis to one sample?
interview.answer: `sample[np.newaxis, ...]` or `expand_dims(sample, 0)`, giving shape `(1, ...)` that a batched model accepts.

interview.q: Why does `ravel()` sometimes copy?
interview.answer: When the memory layout cannot be traversed in the requested order with strides, it must materialise a contiguous copy.

defense.q: Defend `reshape(-1)` at the end of a feature pipeline.
defense.answer: It states that the flattened length is whatever the data implies, so a changed batch size does not break the call.

defense.q: Explain why `concatenate` needs matching ranks.
defense.answer: It joins along an existing axis, so every operand must have the same number of axes and match on the others. `stack` is the operation that adds an axis.

defense.q: Defend storing images as `(N, H, W, C)`.
defense.answer: Channels last keeps each pixel's channels adjacent, which matches how most image decoders write memory and what many frameworks accept.

interview.q: Is `np.add(a, b)` different from `a + b`?
interview.answer: No: `+` calls the same ufunc. The explicit form matters when you need ufunc methods or an `out` buffer.

interview.q: How do you apply a ufunc per row instead of globally?
interview.answer: Apply it elementwise as usual, then reduce with the ufunc's method, for example `np.add.reduce(arr, axis=1)`.

interview.q: Why does `np.divide` return `inf` on a zero denominator instead of raising?
interview.answer: A ufunc processes a whole buffer and cannot abort on one element, so it follows IEEE semantics and warns.

defense.q: Defend wrapping a risky division in `np.errstate`.
defense.answer: It states that division by zero is expected here, so the warning is suppressed deliberately rather than flooding logs. The handling stays local.

defense.q: Explain why `np.abs` on a boolean array is meaningless.
defense.answer: A boolean has no magnitude beyond true or false, so the operation either errors or silently converts. Use the values you actually mean.

defense.q: Defend `np.clip` over an `if` per element.
defense.answer: One vectorised call replaces a Python loop and handles both bounds consistently, including for non-finite inputs.

interview.q: What happens when a `(2, 3)` array is added to a `(3,)` array?
interview.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis and is reused for both rows, producing `(2, 3)`.

interview.q: Why can a scalar broadcast against any shape?
interview.answer: It has no axes to conflict with, so it applies to every element.

interview.q: How do you build an outer product with broadcasting?
interview.answer: Make one operand a column and the other a row, `a[:, None] * b[None, :]`, and the result is the full grid.

defense.q: Defend writing shapes in comments beside broadcast arithmetic.
defense.answer: The same expression means different things for `(n,)` and `(n, 1)`, and a comment makes the intended axis explicit for the next reader.

defense.q: Explain why a column times a row is not a dot product.
defense.answer: Broadcasting multiplies every pair and keeps both axes, while a dot product contracts the shared axis into one number.

defense.q: Defend reshaping explicitly before an operation that relies on broadcasting.
defense.answer: An explicit shape states which axis is being aligned, so a later data change fails loudly instead of broadcasting in the wrong direction.

interview.q: What does `keepdims=True` preserve, and why does it help?
interview.answer: It keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array.

interview.q: How do you normalise each row by its own mean in one expression?
interview.answer: `arr - arr.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)`, which aligns the row means with the rows.

interview.q: Why is `argmin` ambiguous on ties?
interview.answer: It returns the first occurrence by position, so several equal minima report only one index.

defense.q: Defend reporting mean together with standard deviation.
defense.answer: A mean alone hides spread, and two datasets with the same mean can behave completely differently. The pair is the minimum honest summary.

defense.q: Explain why a percentile is not a mean band.
defense.answer: A percentile is a position in the sorted data and tolerates skew; mean plus standard deviation assumes a roughly symmetric spread.

defense.q: Defend naming the axis that disappears when you choose `axis`.
defense.answer: Axis errors are silent, and saying "rows collapse" out loud makes `axis=0` the obvious choice rather than a guess.

interview.q: What is the difference between `arr > 5` and `arr[arr > 5]`?
interview.answer: The first is the boolean mask; the second applies it and returns only the selected values.

interview.q: How do you invert a boolean mask?
interview.answer: Use `~mask`, the elementwise negation, which keeps the array shape.

interview.q: Why do mask expressions need parentheses?
interview.answer: `&` binds tighter than comparison, so `a > 1 & a < 3` compares against the result of the bitwise operation. Parenthesise each comparison.

defense.q: Defend `np.where` over assignment through a mask for three-way choices.
defense.answer: `where` returns a complete new array from two branches, so no element is left in an intermediate state and the intent is one expression.

defense.q: Explain why a mask of the wrong length raises.
defense.answer: The mask maps one-to-one onto positions of an axis, so a different length has no defined alignment. Failing is better than guessing.

defense.q: Defend `np.isin` for filtering against a whitelist.
defense.answer: It answers the whole array in one operation and stays fast for large lists, unlike a per-element Python membership loop.

interview.q: How do you sort a 2-D array by its second column?
interview.answer: Take the order from `np.argsort(arr[:, 1])` and apply it, `arr[order]`, which reorders whole rows.

interview.q: What does `argsort` do with equal values by default?
interview.answer: It uses an unstable algorithm, so tied values may come back in any order unless you request `kind="stable"`.

interview.q: Why is searching a sorted array faster?
interview.answer: A sorted array supports binary search, so the position is found in logarithmically many steps instead of a linear scan.

defense.q: Defend `np.sort` over `list.sort` for a numeric column.
defense.answer: `np.sort` works on the typed buffer with no Python comparisons and returns an array ready for further vectorised work.

defense.q: Explain why `np.unique` returns sorted values.
defense.answer: Sorting is how it detects duplicates efficiently, and a sorted result is deterministic and searchable afterwards.

defense.q: Defend keeping the index array returned by `argsort`.
defense.answer: Sorting values alone loses which row they came from. The index array is what lets labels and features stay aligned.

interview.q: What does `arr.base` tell you?
interview.answer: It points at the array whose buffer this one borrows, and is `None` when this array owns its data.

interview.q: Why do C and Fortran order have different strides?
interview.answer: C order walks the last axis fastest, Fortran the first, so the byte step per axis differs even for the same shape.

interview.q: How can a copy hide a memory bug?
interview.answer: A copy breaks the link between two names, so a write that should be visible through an alias silently is not.

defense.q: Defend copying a function argument before mutating it.
defense.answer: Callers pass views and expect their data intact; mutating in place makes the function's effect depend on aliasing they cannot see.

defense.q: Explain why a transpose followed by a reshape may copy.
defense.answer: After the transpose, the logical order no longer matches memory order, so flattening needs a real copy to produce the requested sequence.

defense.q: Defend checking `nbytes` before loading a file.
defense.answer: The size on disk predicts the memory the array needs, and discovering a 20 GB allocation at load time is worse than refusing early.

interview.q: What is a generator's state, and why pass one around?
interview.answer: It is the internal position in the random stream. Passing the object keeps draws reproducible and independent of any global state.

interview.q: How do you draw reproducible batches in a training loop?
interview.answer: Create one seeded generator and keep calling it; each batch advances the same stream in a fixed order.

interview.q: Why are `random` floats in `[0, 1)` and not `[0, 1]`?
interview.answer: The upper bound is exclusive so the result is uniform over a half-open interval and never equals 1.0, which scaling relies on.

defense.q: Defend fixed seeds in tests but varying seeds in training.
defense.answer: Tests need identical inputs to be meaningful, while training benefits from different sampling each run. Both follow from owning the generator explicitly.

defense.q: Explain why `shuffle` changes the caller's array.
defense.answer: It permutes in place, so every reference to that buffer sees the new order. Use `permutation` when a new array is wanted.

defense.q: Defend `choice` with probabilities for weighted sampling.
defense.answer: It states the weights directly and samples accordingly, instead of building a duplicated pool whose size can explode.

interview.q: What shapes does `np.dot` require for matrices?
interview.answer: The inner dimensions must match: `(m, k)` with `(k, n)` gives `(m, n)`.

interview.q: Why is `@` preferred to `np.dot` for matrix products?
interview.answer: It is the dedicated matrix operator, it reads like the maths, and it does not change meaning for higher-rank inputs the way `dot` does.

interview.q: What does `np.linalg.norm` measure with no arguments?
interview.answer: The Euclidean (Frobenius for matrices) norm, the square root of the sum of squares.

defense.q: Defend verifying a solve with `allclose` rather than equality.
defense.answer: Floating-point factorisation introduces rounding, so exact equality fails even for a correct answer. A tolerance states the accuracy expected.

defense.q: Explain why an identity matrix is used to test a multiplication.
defense.answer: Multiplying by the identity must return the operand, so any deviation isolates a bug in the multiplication or the shape handling.

defense.q: Defend storing a factorisation instead of an inverse.
defense.answer: The factorisation is stable, can be reused for many right-hand sides, and never forms the numerically worse inverse.

interview.q: What does `np.save` add to the file name you give it?
interview.answer: It appends `.npy` when the name does not already end in it, which is why a later `open` of the bare name fails.

interview.q: How do you store several arrays in one file under names?
interview.answer: Use `np.savez` or `np.savez_compressed` with keyword arguments, then read them back by key from the loaded archive.

interview.q: Why does `np.load` require `allow_pickle=False` on untrusted files?
interview.answer: Pickled payloads can execute constructors, so loading becomes code execution. Array-only files need no pickle at all.

defense.q: Defend storing a checksum beside a saved array.
defense.answer: Binary corruption is silent until the numbers are wrong, so a checksum turns a bad file into a clear failure at load time.

defense.q: Explain why CSV is a poor intermediate format.
defense.answer: It loses dtype and exact precision, costs parsing time, and cannot represent several arrays in one file without conventions.

defense.q: Defend `usecols` when reading a wide CSV.
defense.answer: Reading only the needed columns saves both parse time and memory, and it documents which fields the pipeline actually depends on.

interview.q: How do you read one field of a structured array?
interview.answer: Index it by name, `arr["qty"]`, which returns a typed array for that field.

interview.q: What does a unit of `"M"` in a `datetime64` mean?
interview.answer: The value is stored as a count of whole months, so day-level information is not available at that unit.

interview.q: Why do string arrays have a fixed width?
interview.answer: The dtype fixes each element to a number of characters so the buffer can stay contiguous; longer strings are truncated.

defense.q: Defend parsing dates at the boundary rather than mid-pipeline.
defense.answer: One parse converts text to a typed value that arithmetic understands, and later stages never re-guess formats.

defense.q: Explain why a structured array is not a DataFrame.
defense.answer: It stores typed records but has no index, alignment, or per-column methods. It is the compact storage a frame may build on.

defense.q: Defend `object` dtype as a last resort.
defense.answer: It stores Python pointers, so it loses the buffer and vectorised speed. It is acceptable only for genuinely heterogeneous values.

interview.q: What is the difference between NaN and None in an array?
interview.answer: NaN is a float value that means "not a number" and propagates through arithmetic; None is a Python object that forces an object dtype and does not.

interview.q: Why does `nanmean` warn on an all-NaN slice?
interview.answer: There is no value left to average, so it returns NaN and warns that the result is not a real mean.

interview.q: How do you detect infinity?
interview.answer: Use `np.isinf`, optionally with `np.isfinite` to count only usable values.

defense.q: Defend failing loudly on unexpected NaN in a metric.
defense.answer: A NaN silently poisons an average or a comparison, and a metric that reports NaN late is harder to trace than a guard at the start.

defense.q: Explain why `nan_to_num` needs explicit replacement values.
defense.answer: Any default is a modelling decision; stating the value records what missing data became instead of leaving it implicit.

defense.q: Defend tracking missing-value counts as a metric.
defense.answer: The count reveals ingestion problems that an imputed value would hide, and it is cheap to compute alongside the data.

interview.q: What does `np.vectorize` actually do?
interview.answer: It loops in Python and calls your function per element, adding broadcasting as a convenience. It does not compile anything.

interview.q: Why is `np.einsum` often the clearest tensor operation?
interview.answer: It names the indices once, so the contraction, transpose and sum are all visible in one short string instead of three calls.

interview.q: How does `out=` interact with broadcasting?
interview.answer: The output must already have the broadcast result shape; NumPy writes into it and never resizes it.

defense.q: Defend choosing clarity over a hand-tuned ufunc.
defense.answer: An unmeasured optimisation trades readability for an unknown gain. Clarity first, then profile and optimise the hot path.

defense.q: Explain why `np.vectorize` does not make code fast.
defense.answer: The Python call still happens once per element, so the interpreter overhead that dominated the loop remains.

defense.q: Defend setting a memory budget when choosing a vectorised path.
defense.answer: Several vectorised routes compute the same answer with very different peak memory, and the fastest one can still exhaust RAM.

interview.q: What does a model expect from `X.shape`?
interview.answer: Two dimensions: `(n_samples, n_features)`, so each row is one example and each column one feature.

interview.q: Why keep a validation split as an index array?
interview.answer: The same positions can select from features, labels and any aligned table, so the split stays consistent without copying data.

interview.q: Why might converting a DataFrame to an array copy?
interview.answer: Columns with one dtype in one block can be viewed; mixed dtypes must be gathered into a new buffer, which is a copy.

defense.q: Defend NumPy arrays as the interchange format between pipeline stages.
defense.answer: Every stage does numeric work and every framework accepts an array, so a typed contiguous block avoids conversions at each hop.

defense.q: Explain why plotting code should receive arrays rather than frames.
defense.answer: A plot needs x and y vectors, not labels or indexes; passing arrays makes the shape contract explicit and avoids re-parsing the frame.

defense.q: Defend measuring end-to-end time before optimising one stage.
defense.answer: A stage that looks slow may be dominated by loading or conversion elsewhere. Measurement prevents optimising the wrong thing.
